idiom_name: abstract update hook + ordered collection + one per-frame driver walk
implementation_notes: Language-neutral shape: give every live object one update step that takes the frame time as an argument (or reads the engine's frame time) and mutates only its own state; hold the live objects in an ordered collection that the driver walks exactly once per frame. Where the step lives is the main design decision - on the entity class, on a component, or on a delegated state/type object - and the reference form is the abstract hook: a virtual method, an interface or trait member, a function pointer, or a suspension point. What replaces the classic structure: nothing - the hook, the collection and the walk are built from the language's own dispatch mechanism, and the pattern is the discipline around them: dt is passed in rather than read, the order is defined rather than accidental, the collection is not mutated while it is walked (defer spawns and despawns), and dormant objects are kept out of the walk instead of being checked for an enabled flag. At scale, when the per-frame dispatch and pointer chasing dominate, move the behaviour to systems over flat data (Data Locality/ECS) and keep this pattern for the objects that genuinely act independently.
code_sketch:
collection = registry of live objects      # ordered

def frame(dt):
    input.drain()                         # never block
    for obj in collection.walk():         # one driver, one pass
        obj.update(dt)                    # one frame of that object's behaviour
    collection.apply_spawns_and_despawns()  # never mutate during the walk
    render()
pitfalls: The step reads the clock (or a global dt) instead of receiving dt: it can no longer be stepped at a fixed rate or tested in isolation.
The collection is mutated while it is being walked, so spawned objects act immediately and removed objects make the walk skip their neighbours.
Update order is left undefined and objects silently depend on it (A resolving collisions before B), coupling behaviour to registration order.
Dormant objects are walked every frame just to check an enabled flag, wasting dispatch and cache lines instead of keeping an active-object collection.

Wrong move: timing behaviour in frame counts (act when frame % 180 == 0) -> every timer silently changes length at 30 or 144 Hz and during dropped frames -> instead accumulate the dt passed into the step and fire on elapsed-time thresholds.

Wrong move: doing blocking or long synchronous work inside an update step (file or network I/O, generating a whole level at once) -> the driver cannot step any other object or render until the step returns, so the entire world stalls -> instead slice the work across frames, or defer it to a scheduler or worker and keep the step non-blocking.

Wrong move: hiding an expensive one-shot rebuild behind a dirty flag inside the step (recompute the whole navigation mesh when dirty) -> the one frame that clears the flag blows the frame budget for every object -> instead amortise the rebuild in bounded chunks across frames or move it to an explicit async phase.
